item.title: An Army of Paid Creators Is Carpeting the Web With Political Content
item.description:
Judging from his TikTok feed, Drew was struggling to get by as a young man living near Dallas. Grocery bills were skyrocketing, he said, and he was looking for thrift stores to help keep costs down.

In reality, according to his LinkedIn profile, Drew was a man from Utah named Alex Forrester, who said he was now in Florida. “All of it was paid for,” he said in a video posted in late June, which was later deleted. “I don’t even live in Texas,” adding an expletive.

Mr. Forrester, who did not respond to requests for comment, is one of more than 100 content creators identified by The New York Times who in recent months have been paid as much as $30 per post by a progressive group to create videos about affordability for social media.

Similar campaigns this year have paid ordinary people to promote a Republican candidate for Los Angeles mayor, to oppose a regulatory bill pushed by the crypto industry and to call for tighter regulation of artificial intelligence. Early this month, an unidentified nonprofit group offered up to $1,500 for videos on TikTok, YouTube and Instagram that support “mail voting working correctly.”

The accounts posting these messages aren’t run by celebrity influencers with massive engagement, legions of fans and lucrative product endorsement deals. Most have only a smattering of followers and, often, the people behind them aren’t even based in the United States.

Functioning more like birdshot than a single bullet, these high-volume social media campaigns represent the new vanguard of modern political influence, saturating the internet with a topic until it is all but unavoidable. That can help game social media network algorithms so that they treat coordinated content as organic, spreading the message even wider. Built from dozens or hundreds of posts from accounts you’ve never heard of, they amount to an echo chamber on a budget.

“This is digital astroturfing, plain and simple,” said Samuel Woolley, a professor at the University of Pittsburgh who studies how new technologies can be used to manipulate public opinion on the web. “The more people see an idea online, the more inured to it they become and the more commonplace and acceptable it becomes.”

In the political sphere, social media strategies centered around big payments to marquee influencers are still prevalent, with some large accounts taking in $25,000 or more for a single video.

But increasingly, efforts are shifting to content made by smaller freelancers who churn out on-camera videos, slide shows and other material targeting specific audiences.

Some posts, known as user generated content, or U.G.C., feature an individual content creator speaking directly to the camera. Others, referred to in the industry as clipping, consist of short clips taken from longer videos overlaid with text or commentary driving a particular point home.

Such content is rarely marked as paid advertising and, in most cases, laws don’t require any such disclosures for political topics.

One recent campaign, called “Protect What’s Human,” offered $300 or more for posts on Instagram and TikTok that called for “real rules on A.I.” But the job listing made no mention of who funded the effort or any requirement to disclose that it was not organic content. The only obligation was that creators verify that they “have a personal perspective or experience related to how A.I. may affect my work, profession, family, or community.”

“Protect What’s Human” was advertised on a site called People First, one of a growing number of specialized online marketplaces where content creators can look for paid opportunities. Some focus mostly on political advocacy, while others largely feature commercial gigs with a smaller number of political jobs mixed in.

A recent clipping campaign listed on the social commerce platform Whop offered $3 per 1,000 views for short-form videos praising Pierre Poilievre, the conservative leader of Canada’s opposition party. For inspiration, it provided a video of Mr. Poilievre blaming the country’s prime minister for high food prices. Another campaign offered $2 per 1,000 views to promote Maria Syrengela, a member of Greece’s parliament.

A different opportunity on the same marketplace offered even less — $1.50 per 1,000 views — to “join a community of volunteers” working to elect Mike Minogue, the Republican nominee for Massachusetts governor, by cutting videos of the candidate “into compelling 15-60 second clips” posted on social media. The maximum payout for any pro-Minogue post was $150, according to the listing, a tiny fraction of what a big-name social media star would typically charge and an even tinier fraction of the $12.7 million Mr. Minogue has spent so far on television advertising, according to data from tracking firm AdImpact.

“People are sick of paying the insane pricing that typically comes with influencer marketing,” said Drew Levin, a co-founder of SideShift, a popular U.G.C. marketplace, on a podcast last year. “Why spend $1,000 on one video, when you can spend $1,000 on 30 videos?”

Early this year, Project Bullhorn, a Democratic-aligned venture that has said it wants to combat right-wing dominance on social media, turned to SideShift to seek out “U.G.C. creators to speak on the rising crisis of affordability around the United States ahead of the 2026 midterms,” according to a job posting on the site. Initially, it offered $30 per video, but the affordability crisis apparently hit Project Bullhorn as well: That rate recently dropped to $25, the job listing showed.

The Times identified more than 100 social media accounts that took part in Project Bullhorn’s campaign by analyzing the activity of thousands of content creators who signed up with SideShift.

The videos they produced featured creators talking about the high cost of food, fuel and housing around the country; few disclosed they were paid for their posts.

Only a third of the affordability campaign creators appeared to live in the states about which they had posted, according to a Times analysis of participants who had shared their locations.

One man who claimed to be “born and raised” in Texas was actually from Leicestershire, England, according to his profile on SideShift. A woman hired by the campaign to post about affordability in the United States actually lived in Ontario, Canada.

Austin Centre · Austin City

harvtalks

talking about the things that matter! Austin, Texas born and raised

Austin, TX · Austin City

talkswithharv

talking about the things that matter! Austin, Texas📍

Project Bullhorn declined a request for comment. But a person familiar with the campaign who requested anonymity because they were not authorized to speak publicly about the group’s activities said that participating creators are supposed to live in the states that they talk about, or have a close connection to those places, and should be speaking about their own experiences.

Starting in May, creators were offered $1.50 per 1,000 views of videos that combine flattering clips of Ron DeSantis, the Republican governor of Florida, with scripted captions like “DeSantis not holding back 🔥” and “This DeSantis clip has me 😮” on TikTok, YouTube and Instagram.

A detailed set of instructions laid out guidelines for what to do — and what not to do. The golden rule? “Can’t make Ron look bad.”

Mr. DeSantis is term-limited as governor and not currently running for any other office. The job listing does not say who paid for the campaign, but the digital marketing agency Clipping Culture, which posted the ad, stated on its website that the campaign generated more than 6 million views from 1,441 videos.

A review found that a number of those videos appeared to have been made by accounts based overseas. A video featuring Joe Rogan appearing to react to a clip of Mr. DeSantis that included one of the suggested captions was posted by an account that was created in April and is based in Pakistan. Mr. DeSantis’s office did not respond to a request for comment.

dragoni7372

Because clipping campaigns rarely feature the face or voice of the account holder and they tend to pay less per post than U.G.C. content, they often attract creators in other countries, many of whom operate multiple accounts.

A recent report in The Atlantic, for example, found a pro-Republican clipping campaign called Elephant Clipping that paid $3 for every 1,000 views. The instructions stated that “the goal is to showcase how modern conservative figures approach issues such the economy, foreign policy, public safety, education and community development.”

A Times review of accounts posting the suggested content included ones from Nigeria and India; one based in Pakistan used the name Trump in its handle and was created in July.

During his unsuccessful run for Los Angeles mayor this spring, Spencer Pratt, a Republican, paid two clipping firms a total of more than $55,000 to promote his campaign; one of the firms, Cliphaus, boasts on its website that its efforts generated over 50 million views.

“Spencer went from celebrity to serious candidate in the public conversation,” the Cliphaus site says. A Times review found accounts supporting Mr. Pratt based in India, Turkey, and the Philippines. Cliphaus, which is based in Los Angeles, brags of having a “network of 50,000+ independent creators.”

In a statement, ClipHaus co-founder Peter Sint said the firm “operates a global creator network, so creators and publishers participating on the platform may be based in different countries.” He added that “clients can choose specific geographies to target (i.e., U.S.-based accounts only). When it comes to most clients, this is the case.”

Jafari Jackson, a content creator based in Arizona, said he has participated in several campaigns he found on DrumBeat, another marketplace specializing in paid advocacy work. One, he said, pushed the idea that “extreme heat is a climate problem, not a political one,” while another called for content opposing the Save Our Bacon Act, legislation that would roll back state level animal welfare protections.

In recent weeks, DrumBeat hosted a campaign opposing President Trump’s efforts to restrict voting by mail that was sponsored by an unnamed nonprofit that “works to advance policies that support former U.S. service members and their families” and paid $5 per 1,000 views. Another, opposing the Clarity Act, a bill in Congress that would create business-friendly rules for cryptocurrencies, paid $250 per post and suggested scripted talking points including “if a financial system can be used to move money, it needs rules that help investigators stop trafficking and fraud.” (Last week the Senate blocked the bill.)

Mr. Jackson said that he doesn’t bother applying to the vast majority of paid campaigns advertised on DrumBeat, because he “wouldn’t make a video about something I didn’t believe in.”

But he said other creators might find it hard to turn down such opportunities. “While I do think that people should be 100 percent honest in these things,” he said, “it’s hard not to acknowledge the role money plays.”

Andrea Fuller contributed reporting.

item.title: Trump Officials Eject 750,000 From Obamacare Markets, Claiming Fraud
item.description:
The Trump administration has ejected more than 750,000 enrollees from the Affordable Care Act insurance marketplaces, Vice President JD Vance announced on Tuesday, claiming that many were receiving premium subsidies they did not qualify for and that some were not real people.

“We’re actually making sure that the people receiving Obamacare subsidies are actually entitled to receive them,” Mr. Vance said at a news conference, using a different name for the health law. He estimated that removing the targeted enrollees would save the government $2.2 billion.

The announcement was the latest initiative by an anti-fraud task force Mr. Vance leads that has often turned its efforts toward federal health programs. In recent months, the task force has been involved in withholding billions in Medicaid funding from Minnesota and California, contending that the states had not adequately combated fraud.

Obamacare enrollment has already declined significantly this year, as the cost of the plans has risen, a potential political risk for Republicans heading into midterm elections in which voters are worried about affordability and the cost of living.

Congressional Democrats immediately criticized the Trump administration’s announcement on Tuesday as an unjustified move to dismantle Affordable Care Act, known as Obamacare.

“Using the false pretext of fighting fraud to strip Americans of their healthcare is as cynical as it is cruel,” Representative Nancy Pelosi, Democrat of California, posted on social media.

The dropped enrollees account for about 4 percent of the 19 million Americans who receive coverage through the marketplaces created by the Affordable Care Act. Many live close to the poverty line.

Under the law, people who earn more than four times the poverty limit — around $64,000 for a single person — are ineligible for subsidies to help them afford premiums. But people who earn less than the federal poverty limit — around $16,000 a year — are also ineligible. The lawmakers who wrote Obamacare had intended that such people would obtain health insurance through an expansion of Medicaid, before the Supreme Court made Medicaid coverage for this low-income group optional for states.

The Trump administration asked health plans to verify eligibility for nearly 1.2 million people who were signed up by a broker and missing a Social Security number or immigration papers, according to a spokesperson for the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services, which oversees Obamacare.

Officials then narrowed that list to people who had not filed insurance claims, had no record of contacting the insurer about the coverage and whose premiums were fully covered by government subsidies.

Obamacare enrollees had 30 days to respond to their insurers. Those who were flagged under the criteria and did not respond to their health plan’s outreach had their coverage canceled.

The spokesperson said that if a “legitimate consumer” believed he or she was affected by the cancellations, the person could get coverage reinstated by providing the Obamacare marketplace with their Social Security number.

Mr. Vance said the 750,000 who would lose coverage were a mix of people who did not meet the eligibility requirements or did not exist.

Officials said they planned to investigate an additional 440,000 enrollees who may also fall into one of those categories.

“They had something about their story that was a little bit different than what we expected from the 100 percent fraud story,” Dr. Mehmet Oz, the administrator of the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services, said of the Obamacare enrollees the administration would allow to remain enrolled. “We’re giving them another chance.”

In statements, two large insurance industry groups, America’s Health Insurance Plans and the Blue Cross Blue Shield Association, said they welcomed efforts to reduce fraud in the marketplaces.

There is evidence that ineligible low-income people have enrolled in coverage in recent years, either because they overestimated their expected income or because a broker coached them to do so to obtain coverage. The Congressional Budget Office estimates that there were around 2.3 million such people in 2025.

There is also evidence that some insurance brokers, who earn commissions for each enrollment, illegally signed people up for coverage without their knowledge, though the number of such people is estimated to be substantially lower. During the Biden administration, health officials decertified around 200 brokers after learning they were engaged in such behavior — in many cases switching people from the plan they chose to another plan to harvest commissions. The Trump administration recertified those brokers last year, but has since removed more brokers from the program.

“We absolutely found that there was a fair amount of unauthorized activity,” said Ellen Montz, who oversaw the Obamacare marketplaces for the Biden administration. She described an uptick in fraudulent enrollments that started in 2024, and said that in response, the Biden administration cracked down on brokers and began requiring more documents during online enrollment.

At the news conference, Dr. Oz focused on fraudulent broker rings and announced a six-month moratorium on new brokers selling Obamacare policies. He highlighted the case of two Florida brokers who had been found guilty of bribing homeless people to enroll in Obamacare plans, so they could earn commissions. Both were sentenced in February to 20 years of jail time.

Cynthia Cox, the director of a program on the Affordable Care Act at KFF, a health research group, said that the administration’s action appeared to fall outside the normal process for verifying eligibility. “There is widespread agreement that unauthorized enrollments should be canceled,” she said. “The question is whether these were all indeed unauthorized enrollments and whether this was the appropriate process for determining whether an enrollee was legitimate or not.”

Ms. Cox and Ms. Montz both noted that problems with the data of enrollees did not necessarily constitute fraud.

“I would absolutely foresee that totally legitimate enrollments are going to get cut off here,” Ms. Montz said.

Enrollment in coverage sold in the Affordable Care Act marketplaces had already fallen by several million this year, after Congress declined to extend temporary funding that had made coverage less expensive. Prices rose substantially, and many low-income Americans lost access to free coverage. Early filings from insurers suggest that prices will increase substantially again next year. The sign-up period will begin days before the midterm congressional election.

Though there is little current data on the uninsured rate now, estimates from the C.B.O. and other analysts suggest that most of the lower-income people who have lost Obamacare coverage will remain uninsured.

The Paragon Health Institute, a right-leaning research group with close ties to the administration, has published reports estimating that more than a quarter of Obamacare enrollees were improperly signed up. The research noted disproportionate sign-ups among low-income enrollees, enrollments with missing data, and a subset of enrollees who never made medical claims. That research helped inform changes in how people sign up for coverage that were passed into law last year as part of the large Republican tax bill. But those changes do not kick in until after the election.

The administration also tried to add new requirements to the enrollment process through regulation, but the changes have been stopped by a court.

item.title: Federal Judge Sets Hearing for Venezuelan Man Shot by ICE in Austin
item.description:
A federal judge has scheduled a hearing to determine whether a Venezuelan man shot by an immigration agent in Austin on Sunday should be deported as concerns persist about his medical care in custody, his lawyer said Tuesday.

The man, Wilber Rafael Garces Perez, 28, was taken from a detention center to a hospital in San Antonio after he complained that he was not able to move his left arm, said his lawyer, Kate Lincoln-Goldfinch.

Mr. Garces Perez was released from the hospital at midnight and is now back at the deportation center in Pearsall, Texas, where a bullet remains lodged near the back of his neck, Ms. Lincoln-Goldfinch said. Mr. Garces Perez has not been told why doctors have not removed the bullet, she added.

“They shackled him yesterday in waist chains and handcuffs and ankle chains, and took him to the hospital in San Antonio, where they gave him a morphine drip and tended to his wound,” Ms. Lincoln-Goldfinch said. “He is currently only on Tylenol, ibuprofen, and he reports that he’s in isolation.”

Court records show that Mr. Garces Perez had asked a federal judge to block his deportation and order his release. U.S. District Judge Orlando L. Garcia of the Western District of Texas scheduled a hearing for Sept. 30 and ordered Mr. Garces Perez to appear in person.

On Monday, Mr. Garces Perez called into a news conference from the detention center and said that he had felt only one gunshot enter his body after a federal officer shot him during a traffic stop Sunday afternoon while delivering food for DoorDash.

Mr. Garces Perez said that he had been bleeding and was in pain, but was released from a hospital hours after he was wounded. He that a doctor had told him that agents from Immigration and Customs Enforcement were in a hurry to take him to detention.

Representatives from D.H.S. and ICE on Tuesday did not respond to questions about Mr. Garces Perez’s account. It is unclear if the agent was wearing a body cam.

The episode unfolded Sunday in northwest Austin, as ICE agents checking license plates discovered that Mr. Garces Perez had a deportation order on file.

Agents told Mr. Garces Perez that they were ICE agents and that he was going to be arrested, according to two people granted anonymity because they were not authorized to discuss the investigation. Mr. Garces Perez then fled in his car.

A short chase ensued before ICE agents encountered Mr. Garces Perez again. He did not appear to be the target of a federal investigation before the encounter, the two people said.

During the news conference Monday afternoon, Mr. Garces Perez told reporters that he had been making a delivery when an S.U.V. had tried to hit his car. He said he thought it was an aggressive driver and kept driving. Mr. Garces Perez then said the S.U.V. then hit his vehicle and turned on police lights after the collision. He was shot after the car was stopped.

The shooting was the second in Texas by an ICE agent since July and the latest in a string of similar episodes involving federal immigration agents across the nation. More than 20 people have been shot at by ICE since President Trump took office last year, nearly all in cars, and some fatally.

The Homeland Security Investigations unit of D.H.S. and the Federal Bureau of Investigation are leading the investigation into the shooting of Mr. Garces Perez, a spokesman for D.H.S. said. The local district attorney is also investigating.

Calls for an independent investigation continue to grow. More than 100 members of Congress signed a letter that demanded Mr. Garces Perez receive proper medical care and called for his release. The letter also called for the release of unedited video footage of the encounter and other evidence.

Mr. Garces Perez has told his immigration lawyer that he entered the United States in 2024 seeking asylum and later got a work permit. At one point, he changed his address, and a hearing notice was sent to his former home. He didn’t know that he had an immigration hearing and did not go, which led to the deportation order, his attorney said.

item.title: F.B.I. Shut Down Inquiry Into Top Ally of Senator Susan Collins
item.description:
The F.B.I. in 2025 shut down an inquiry into allegations that a political adviser to Senator Susan Collins had participated in a scheme to funnel illegal campaign contributions from a defense contractor seeking lucrative federal contracts, current and former officials said.

The bureau began investigating the matter under the Biden administration, after Martin Kao, the chief executive of Navatek, a military contractor in Hawaii, said he had discussed circumventing campaign finance laws with a political adviser to Ms. Collins, Republican of Maine. Mr. Kao is now serving an 87-month prison sentence for wire fraud, money laundering and bank fraud, some of which related to a separate scheme to defraud the government of pandemic aid money.

The inquiry, which was earlier reported by ProPublica, was closed under the Trump administration last year because senior bureau officials questioned the veracity of Mr. Kao’s account, which he began offering around the time he pleaded guilty in 2022.

Current and former officials familiar with the investigation, who spoke on the condition of anonymity to describe a sensitive inquiry, said agents did not uncover much evidence to corroborate Mr. Kao’s claims against the senator and her advisers, including Scott Reed, a fund-raiser for Ms. Collins. But they acknowledged that it was possible more could have surfaced if the investigation had developed further.

The disclosure of the inquiry and its closing came in the final weeks of a midterm election in which Ms. Collins is in a tight race that could help decide control of the Senate. It prompted accusations that the F.B.I.’s decision to shut down the investigation last year was influenced by political considerations — safeguarding a critical seat that could decide which party controls the Senate.

On Capitol Hill, Ms. Collins pushed back against the article, calling it “truly outrageous.”

“These are seven-year-old allegations that were thoroughly investigated by the Biden Justice Department and F.B.I. And in 2021, the Biden Justice Department found there was no wrongdoing by any one on my campaign staff, my office or me,” she said. “It is clearly a political hit job.”

“It is very frustrating and unfair to have it brought up this close to the election,” she added, noting that the man at the center of the accusations is a twice-convicted felon.

“He is a liar and that is what he is doing here,” she said.

Annie Clark, Ms. Collins’s deputy chief of staff, described the allegations against the senator and her advisers as “categorically false.” In a lengthy social media post on Tuesday morning, she said that her campaign “cooperated fully with the F.B.I. throughout the investigation, producing all of the documents it requested and serving as fact witnesses in official settings.”

“As Martin Kao was awaiting sentencing, he began making outlandish charges about the Collins office, deflecting blame from himself and placing it on Senator Collins,” she wrote, adding: “The FBI and the Court obviously did not believe Kao.”

In an email to ProPublica, Ms. Clark added that the campaign ultimately returned the money. The committee sent the donations to a group that was rebuilding a school in Frenchville, Maine, that burned down in 2021, according to a person with knowledge of the move.

In President Trump’s second term, the Justice Department has scuttled the main unit responsible for investigating public corruption, while dropping investigations against Republicans and Trump allies, including Eric Adams, the former mayor of New York.

Kash Patel, the F.B.I. director, also fired many agents in a public corruption unit at the Washington field office that had handled the Kao inquiry who had gone on to work for the special counsel Jack Smith, including one of the agents who had investigated Mr. Kao.

Ms. Collins, a moderate, is not close to Mr. Trump and has often sought to distance herself from some of his policies.

Mr. Kao told investigators that executives with his company had met in 2019 with Mr. Reed, who asked them for a large donation even though federal law prohibits direct contributions from federal contractors, according to ProPublica’s account, which was later confirmed by two former officials.

Mr. Kao said he was willing to do so provided Ms. Collins’s team could ensure the company received millions in naval contracts in Maine. As a workaround, Mr. Kao created a shell company and sent a $150,000 check to a super PAC associated with Ms. Collins, ProPublica reported.

Around the same time, Navatek received an $8 million contract for a boat hull research project. Ms. Collins visited the company’s offices in Maine to celebrate the deal, posting a photograph of herself on Facebook holding a model boat and standing next to Mr. Kao.

Ms. Collins, 73, faces what is arguably the toughest re-election campaign of her three-decade career as a Republican representing a blue state.

Her Democratic opponent, Troy Jackson, the former speaker of Maine’s State Senate, seized on the disclosure of the F.B.I. investigation to accuse Ms. Collins of corruption and to cast Mr. Trump as her political wingman.

“Susan Collins delivered millions in taxpayer dollars for a corrupt donor bankrolling her campaign, and then Donald Trump helped her cover it up,” he said in a fund-raising email sent on Tuesday.

Ben Williamson, a spokesman for the bureau, said it had investigated claims against Ms. Collins and “found nothing” indicating that the senator or her campaign had done anything illegal. “Any suggestion otherwise is totally false.”

Carl Hulse contributed reporting.

item.title: Federal Judge Orders Texas to Air-Condition Its Prisons
item.description:
Texas must fully air-condition its prisons by the end of 2029, a federal judge ordered on Tuesday, saying the lack of cooling in most lockups in the sun-blasted state violates the U.S. Constitution’s ban on cruel and unusual punishment.

The ruling from U.S. District Court Judge Robert Pitman was a major victory for prisoners’ rights advocates, who have complained for decades about poor conditions behind bars.

In his 150-page order, Judge Pitman said that the Texas Department of Criminal Justice, which operates the country’s largest prison system, had “failed to act with reasonable urgency or commitment to install air conditioning.”

“In a state where outdoor heat indexes exceed 130 degrees, inmates in Texas prisons are suffering — and in some cases dying — in extreme heat every summer,” Judge Pitman wrote.

This is a developing story. Check back for updates.

Lauren McGaughy contributed reporting.

item.title: Supreme Court Order Gives Parents Custody of Baby in Surrogacy Fight
item.description:
Justice Elena Kagan on Tuesday refused to intervene in a high-profile custody battle that involved difficult questions surrounding surrogacy and abortion, leaving in place a lower-court order that gave custody to the biological parents in the dispute.

The case drew national attention when a surrogate from Alaska refused to have an abortion after the fetus she was carrying was diagnosed with a serious heart problem. She eventually traveled to Texas and gave birth to the child over the initial objections of the parents, a couple from California.

The baby boy was born in August. He received open-heart surgery and has been in a pediatric intensive care unit at a hospital in Dallas, where the couple have also been living to be with him.

On Tuesday, Justice Kagan, who oversees emergency filings from California, denied the surrogate’s request to block the lower-court ruling in the couple’s favor. She acted on her own without referring the matter to her Supreme Court colleagues. The justice’s order did not include an explanation, as is often the case when the court responds to such filings.

The couple, Nausheen Gilkar and Omar Ahmed, had struggled to have a baby and entered into a surrogacy arrangement with McKenna West, a nurse. Their legal dispute began in April after the fetus was diagnosed with hypoplastic left heart syndrome at around 20 weeks of pregnancy.

The rare and life-threatening congenital heart condition requires open-heart surgery soon after birth, followed by two additional childhood heart surgeries.

The couple asked Ms. West to terminate the pregnancy, citing a provision of their contract with her that left decisions dealing with abortion to them. Ms. West refused. She later moved to Texas, where the boy was born on Aug. 12.

Ms. West is represented by the Alliance Defending Freedom, a conservative Christian legal organization whose lawyers appear frequently before the Supreme Court. The Texas attorney general, Ken Paxton, also intervened in state court to ensure the child received medical treatments. He later dropped out of the case.

In June, a California court recognized Ms. Gilkar and Mr. Ahmed as the boy’s parents. A judge in Texas extended a temporary order barring Ms. West from presenting herself as a parent to the baby.

After a subsequent court hearing in Texas, a judge directed the hospital in Dallas to provide lifesaving care and prohibited the baby’s removal from Texas. On Sept. 2, the court also dismissed Ms. West from the proceeding.

In their emergency request, Ms. West’s lawyers told the Supreme Court that she had been denied “control over the medically fragile child.” Without intervention from the justices, they said, “she will receive no further information about the child she carried for 37 weeks and fought to save.”

The case should have been resolved in Alaska, her lawyers said, adding that the California courts had stripped Ms. West of her rights to “protect the baby’s life.”

In response, lawyers for the couple said on Friday that they have ensured that “their child receives the lifesaving care he needs — and they are committed to doing so for the rest of his life.”

An order from the Supreme Court blocking state court decisions would allow Ms. West to be involved in the child’s medical care and “serve only to cause chaos and confusion,” according to the heavily redacted filing.

Ms. Gilkar and Mr. Ahmed are “providing the precise medical care for their child” that Ms. West desires, the lawyers said, adding that “a right to life is not at issue here.”

The relationship between the couple and the surrogate got off to a smooth start. Ms. West stayed with them when she met with fertility doctors in California. Ms. Gilkar said in state court proceedings in Texas that she had sat by Ms. West’s side during the procedure transferring the embryo — biologically Ms. Gilkar’s and Mr. Ahmed’s — so that Ms. West could carry it to term.

But now they are at odds over even what to call the child. Ms. Gilkar and Mr. Ahmed named him Rumi, which their lawyer said had been put on his birth certificate. Ms. West’s lawyers used a different name, Gabriel, chosen by Ms. West, until they were told by the Texas judge to stop.

In response to the Supreme Court’s order on Tuesday, Ms. West’s lawyer, Lincoln Davis Wilson, said his client is disappointed in the ruling, but “takes great comfort in how these legal proceedings have prompted the contracting parents to say they are committed to provide the baby with the lifesaving care he needs. That’s what McKenna has been fighting for from day one.”

The couple’s lawyer, Adam Wolf, said they are “truly grateful that Rumi can continue receiving the treatment he needs to survive, and that he will not be stripped away from what has been described by doctors as the excellent care of his parents.”

item.title: Republican Senator Urges Congress to Investigate Donald Trump Jr.
item.description:
A Republican senator on Tuesday called for the Senate to investigate whether Donald Trump Jr., the president’s eldest son, exploited his access to his father for personal gain, spurred by reports that a Russian oligarch funded a lavish wedding after-party for the younger Mr. Trump.

In a three-page letter, Senator John Curtis, Republican of Utah, urged the Judiciary Committee to subpoena Donald Trump Jr., after it was revealed that a Russian businessman with ties to the Kremlin paid hundreds of thousands of dollars for the festivities on an island in the Bahamas this year.

Issuing such a subpoena would be exceedingly unlikely by the Republican-led panel, and top Republicans would not say on Tuesday whether they planned to take action. But the request by Mr. Curtis marked a rare instance of a G.O.P. lawmaker daring to challenge the president.

The president has said that his son would repay the Russian businessman, Umar Kremlev, for what he called a wedding gift. But Mr. Curtis rejected that characterization.

“A toaster is a wedding gift,” the senator said in a social media post. “A private-island party paid for by a Putin-connected oligarch is something else. Republicans nearly wore out the subpoena machine investigating Hunter Biden’s foreign relationships. We should not unplug it now.”

For years, Congress scrutinized President Joseph R. Biden Jr.’s son, Hunter, and whether he milked his connection to his father as a means to bolster his foreign business dealings. In their inquiry, G.O.P. lawmakers looked at whether the younger Mr. Biden's foreign business dealings were inappropriately connected to the president, a claim that he vehemently denied.

On Tuesday, Mr. Curtis pressed lawmakers to look again at Hunter Biden in addition to Mr. Trump’s son. He said the committee should scrutinize foreign actors’ access to the first family and whether “such relationships can create actual or perceived expectations of favorable treatment.”

Since House Republicans issued a criminal referral against him in 2024, Hunter Biden was pardoned by his father. In response to Mr. Curtis’s request on Tuesday, he said: “Bring it on.”

The Utah Republican’s call for an inquiry came as a growing group of Republicans has become more emboldened about breaking with the president ahead of November’s elections. Representative Ashley Hinson of Iowa, a Republican running for the Senate, called on Mr. Trump on Monday to end the war with Iran. That came just days after two other G.O.P. lawmakers from Iowa who are battling for re-election, Representatives Zach Nunn and Mariannette Miller-Meeks, crossed party lines to help push through a Democratic measure directing Mr. Trump to halt the conflict.

Such dissent has placed Republican leaders in a difficult position.

Senator Chuck Grassley of Iowa, the chairman of the Judiciary Committee, said on Tuesday that he would take Mr. Curtis’s request seriously but added that such requests take time.

“If you were going to ask me when you’re going to have a hearing, there’s no way I could answer that today,” Mr. Grassley said.

Senator John Thune of South Dakota, the majority leader, also did not express a view.

“I understand there’s been a request to get some of that information, and you know, Chairman Grassley and the relevant committee would have to make some determinations about that,” Mr. Thune said.

Donald Trump Jr. admitted to accepting gifts from Mr. Kremlev, the president of the International Boxing Association, after ProPublica reported on the arrangement. The festivities he paid for included renting a private island and a fireworks display. The president did not attend the wedding.

Mr. Kremlev has direct ties to President Vladimir V. Putin of Russia. His boxing association is also backed by Gazprom, Russia’s government-owned natural gas company.

Carl Hulse contributed reporting.

item.title: Rollerblading Norwegian Dies After Being Hit by a Car in Kansas
item.description:
A Norwegian man who was seeking to in-line skate across the United States died this month after he was hit by a car in Kansas, according to the authorities and his family.

The skater, identified by the Saline County Sheriff’s Office in Kansas as Joachim Lanham, 24, of Norway, had been documenting his travels on social media. His Instagram bio said he was a “Trans-continental Inline Skater” and “pushing wheels further than they should.”

The Lanham family updated his Instagram account announcing his death with a video from his phone of an orange butterfly resting on a sock-covered foot. The caption says that Mr. Lanham was 22 days into his New-York-to-Los-Angeles journey, which was expected to cover some 2,000 miles.

According to the post, Mr. Lanham was on the outskirts of Salina, Kan., on Sept. 5, where “that afternoon he was hit by a car.”

Brent Melander, the undersheriff of Saline County, said Mr. Lanham had been found unconscious at the side of a two-lane road. He was eventually transferred to the intensive care unit at Wesley Medical Center in Wichita, Kan., where he spent six days before dying from his injuries.

An 82-year-old woman driving an S.U.V. is believed to have been involved in the accident, the authorities said. The investigation has been sent to the Saline County Attorney’s Office for review, according to the sheriff’s office.

In an interview on Tuesday, Mr. Lanham’s brother, Michael Lanham, recalled Joachim’s previous adventures rollerblading, including long distances from Sydney to Perth in Australia, as well as a trek from Oslo to Vienna, among others.

“What he was doing was very unique, not a lot of people are doing what he was doing,” he said.

Michael Lanham said his brother had played hockey growing up but hadn’t liked competition. He had found their father’s Rollerblades in the basement of their home and just “started using them.” Around the time he turned 18 he started skating long distances.

In his social media photos and videos, Mr. Lanham can be seen wearing a bright yellow helmet and reflective gear while rollerblading. Michael Lanham said his brother also had a light on his helmet.

Mr. Lanham’s precise route and daily itineraries were not immediately clear, but his brother said that he had traveled almost 200 kilometers in one day: “199.7, to be exact, that was his longest distance,” he said.

Mr. Lanham had carried with him only the essentials for his adventure, his brother said. He always had a bottle, often filled with his favorite drink, chocolate milk.

“Joachim was doing what he loved and no one was going to stop him,” Michael Lanham said.

item.title: Hospitals Shutter Youth Gender Clinics in Deal With Trump Administration
item.description:
At least six major hospitals across the country have recently agreed to stop providing gender-transition treatment to adolescents to end a wide-ranging Justice Department investigation into potential legal violations related to billing practices and consumer fraud.

The wave of settlements includes hospitals in New York, Pennsylvania and Connecticut, states that have been supportive of access to the treatments. The hospitals have agreed to pay fines, and several will provide free medical care to former patients who wish to treat side effects or to “detransition.”

The agreements are a victory for the Trump administration, which has asserted that the potential harms of gender transition for young people outweigh any benefits and that hospitals have overbilled for transition treatments to make a profit. Since early 2025, the administration has applied an array of financial and legal pressures to health care providers to stop treatments in 24 states that permit them.

Many hospitals had already suspended the treatments, citing pressure from the administration. But legal experts and transgender advocates said the new deals with hospitals add a sense of finality.

In a statement on Friday, Attorney General Todd Blanche said the agreements show that “hospitals that target children in these practices and then fraudulently obtain payment for the procedures will be held to account.” He said the Justice Department was continuing to seek agreements with other hospitals.

Most of the agreements have not been made public. The hospitals that reached agreements as of May and as recently as last week are Texas Children’s Hospital, Cleveland Clinic, Connecticut Children’s Medical Center, Mount Sinai Health System, New York University Langone Hospital and the UPMC Children’s Hospital of Pittsburgh.

Representatives for some of the hospitals said they had reached settlements in order to avoid long legal battles with the federal government, as well as to avoid revealing personal data the government has sought about their patients.

Some critics have argued that the Justice Department was acting in bad faith, raising financial questions to intimidate hospitals into ending services that are permitted in their states and to carry out the Trump administration’s policy goals. The Department of Health and Human Services has proposed a rule that would prevent any federal funding from going to hospitals that provide gender treatments to adolescents, though the rule has yet to take effect.

Others have criticized the hospitals, comparing them to law firms and universities that agreed to Trump administration demands at the expense of patients. One advocacy group, Gender Liberation Movement, has organized protests in recent weeks at Mount Sinai and NYU Langone, two New York City hospitals that have reached agreements with the Justice Department.

“It’s devastating to watch, one by one, health care institutions that once cared for trans youth turn their backs on them,” said Raquel Willis, the organization's executive director.

Several Connecticut families have filed a legal challenge against Connecticut Children’s Medical Center for ending medical care for transgender adolescents last year. The hospital agreed in August that it would keep its gender clinic closed for a decade, pay the government $60,000 and provide $500,000 for patients under the age of 19 who wish to reverse the effects of the treatment, according to a copy of the settlement obtained by The New York Times.

“By agreeing to this settlement, the hospital has doubled down,” Hannah Hussey, a lawyer for the parents, said in a statement. “Not only on that breach of faith with parents and patients, but on its attempt to thwart its obligation under Connecticut law to provide medical care without discrimination.”

A spokeswoman for Connecticut Children’s declined to comment on details of the agreement, but defended it as necessary. “We have reached a resolution that allows our organization to remain focused on our mission of improving the health and well-being of children,” the hospital said in a statement.

Most major medical associations in the United States endorse gender-transition medication for adolescents who experience a mismatch between their sex and their sense of their own gender, known as gender dysphoria. Young people with the diagnosis are at higher risk of depression, anxiety and self-harm as their peers, research shows.

But there are some known risks, including fertility loss and regret, and several reviews by health experts have concluded that the treatments have not been studied well enough to establish whether they are beneficial. The Trump administration has said it is acting on the behalf of young patients and families, which it has portrayed as misled or unequipped to fully consent.

The treatment often includes puberty-delaying medication followed by hormones that align physical traits like body hair and voice range with an adolescent’s gender identity. In rarer cases, it can include surgery.

The Justice Department has said its investigations focus on potential violations of the Food, Drug and Cosmetic Act, the False Claims Act and other federal health care laws. A Health and Human Services report last month suggested that hospitals had incorrectly billed insurers for gender-transition treatment to obtain bigger reimbursements from federal health care programs and private insurers.

But in statements, several hospitals denied any wrongdoing, and legal experts said providing transition care for youths remains legal in about half of U.S. states.

“There has been no determination that offering this care, including to young people, violates any federal law,” said Katie Keith, director of the Health Policy and the Law Initiative at Georgetown University Law Center.

item.title: Blocking Windmills? Banning Press? Building an Arch? Trump Cites National Security.
item.description:
As President Trump tries to barrel through legal and political pushback on fronts ranging from press freedom to his triumphal arch, he is increasingly using a justification he believes will allow him to do what he wants: national security.

The president has cited national security as a reason to build a fancy new ballroom on White House grounds and to investigate leaks to journalists that embarrassed his administration.

He has invoked national security in stripping union rights from thousands of federal workers and deploying the military to the Mexican border to crack down on migrants.

He has cited national security as a reason to pause the construction of wind farms off the East Coast and exempt oil and gas drilling in the Gulf of Mexico from protections for endangered species of whales.

On social media, Mr. Trump has argued that the ban he initiated last week on CNN, MS Now and Politico entering the White House grounds was necessary because they were a “threat to our national security.”

Perhaps nowhere was the reasoning more sudden, or curious, than his announcement on Sunday that he was transforming his plans for a 250-foot triumphal arch on a Washington roundabout, which are under legal challenge.

What was envisioned as a project to honor America’s 250th anniversary, Mr. Trump said, would now also be a military depot, outfitted with “large numbers of drones,” snipers and ammunition. It is unclear what the arch, which would lie between the Lincoln Memorial and Arlington National Cemetery, would protect.

“Courts historically have been deferential to the executive branch in matters of national security, and that is due to the president’s role as commander in chief,” said Barbara McQuade, a University of Michigan Law School professor and a former U.S. attorney. “But it’s not a 100 percent Trump card. If the president invokes the national security rationale frivolously, then he could undermine the power for future presidents who need to invoke it legitimately.”

Mr. Trump has found mixed success in pursuing his national security claims in court.

They featured most prominently in a lawsuit over his ballroom project at the White House. In that case, federal courts distinguished the parts of the project legitimately needed for security, such as an underground bunker, and allowed work on them to proceed, while finding that the aboveground ballroom should be halted without congressional approval. Ultimately, the Supreme Court allowed the entire project to proceed without deciding that issue by dismissing the lawsuit on technical grounds.

Before the president’s surprise announcement, the idea that the arch would have a military or security purpose had not appeared among the administration’s arguments for the project in court. The Justice Department has argued, instead, that the administration is operating under the assumption that it has century-old permission from Congress.

In 1925, Congress passed a bill authorizing construction of the Arlington Memorial Bridge, including a pair of 166-foot-tall columns in the plaza where Memorial Circle is now. Those columns were later dropped from the plans. But the administration has argued that the authority to build them — indeed, to convert them into a far larger arch — still remains.

The administration has gone to great lengths to incorporate that legal logic into the planning, design and public pitch for the project. The main body of the arch is designed to be 166 feet tall, nodding to the earlier proposal. And the National Park Service, which administers the land, has said in documents that it cannot consider relocating the arch somewhere less intrusive because it is “grounded in the historic design intent” for this location.

The administration has effectively spent months tying the legal strategy for the project to this historical story. But the president appeared this week to be shifting strategy, with perplexing consequences.

Public plans for the arch treat it as a tourist attraction, allowing as many 80 people an hour to visit an observation deck offering grand views of the capital. The administration has also been developing new traffic patterns to ease pedestrian access. If the arch is intended, however, to store ammunition, and for its roof to host snipers and drones, it would make little sense to welcome hundreds of tourists a day, since easy access by the public would probably be a security liability.

Federal laws establish requirements for the safe storage of arms, ammunition and explosives that necessitate a level of security at odds with Mr. Trump’s stated desires for the site.

Ammunition would probably need to be placed in an earth-covered bunker — potentially one fully underground beneath the proposed arch — and the entire site would need to be protected with a mix of tall fencing, cameras, intrusion alarms and expensive high-security locks. Firearms could probably be stored inside the arch in what the government calls a ready-service locker.

All of those security devices would have to be certified by the General Services Administration, and the fencing alone would make the site much more difficult for tourists to visit.

If enough ammunition is stored at the site, the project could require the permanent closure of nearby roadways. Those could include the road to the main entrance to Arlington National Cemetery, as well as the George Washington Parkway — a major thoroughfare along the Potomac River that carries more than 70,000 vehicles per day.

A White House spokesman did not respond to specific questions about the changing plans for the arch, except to point to the president’s social media comments.

Ammunition would likely need to be placed in a bunker underground

Representative Donald S. Beyer Jr., a Democrat who represents the Northern Virginia district that includes Arlington National Cemetery, said Mr. Trump’s plan to “make his vanity arch an ammunition depot for ‘snipers’ in a location where snipers have never been needed would place a large weapons cache within feet of thousands of tourists, pedestrians, cyclists and drivers on major commuter traffic thoroughfares and Metro’s Blue Line.”

Mr. Beyer said such a drastic change in the arch’s purpose would “necessitate a redo of all prior impact studies, some of which remain unreleased if they were ever done at all.”

The arch’s location, at a remove from Washington’s highest-value targets, would seemingly also limit its effectiveness for security. Well-trained snipers in the U.S. military can hit targets about three-quarters of a mile away, meaning they could engage a threat only about as far as the Lincoln Memorial, far out of reach of the White House, the Capitol, the Supreme Court, the Pentagon or the bulk of the National Mall.

However, Mr. Trump’s insistence that he would need to launch drones from the arch is undercut by the presence of an active Army post, Fort Myer, about a mile directly west of the site, where such aircraft could be securely stored and deployed.

Kimberly Wehle, a law professor at the University of Baltimore, said Mr. Trump’s push to use national security as a justification for so many actions should be viewed in the broader context of his maximalist approach to executive power, and the push to expand presidential powers in post-9/11 America.

“In Project 2025 and building since then is this idea that the president is actually supposed to function as a de facto sovereign,” Ms. Wehle said. “Donald Trump is taking that idea and imposing it across the board.”

item.title: Trump Once Vowed to ‘Own’ Greenland. He Settled for Something Much Less.
item.description:
In January, President Trump was clear about his need to take over all of Greenland, and to make it American territory. “That’s what I feel is psychologically needed for success,” he said. “Ownership gives you things and elements that you can’t get from just signing a document, that you can have a base.”

On Tuesday, he signed a document that paves the way to expanding the U.S. military presence on the island, opening new bases. But it explicitly stops short of conveying any territory to the United States. And no one — especially Denmark, which governs the vast but mostly empty space — wanted to emphasize that point, for fear that Mr. Trump might renounce the agreement he had just hailed as “tremendous for Europe and for the United States.”

For Mr. Trump, it was a major retreat. He first raised the possibility of buying Greenland during his first term, and never let go of the idea. Even before he was inaugurated, he was making a national security case for making the territory part of the United States, acutely aware that, if he could get it, it would be an acquisition on the scale of President Thomas Jefferson’s Louisiana Purchase.

And few issues did more to galvanize European allies against the Trump administration, especially once they feared that he might make a military move against a NATO ally. There is no evidence he ever seriously considered that step. But that did nothing to alleviate the fears.

Diplomats involved in the process of drafting the 10-page agreement released on Tuesday said they spent months on the language — and then waited for what they hoped would be the right moment to present it to Mr. Trump. And even then they were nervous, acutely aware that after the United States signed an agreement on nuclear energy with Saudi Arabia over the summer, Mr. Trump announced, the next day, that he was changing key terms.

The diplomats spoke on the condition of anonymity to discuss sensitive negotiations.

Whether Mr. Trump has permanently dropped his insistence on owning Greenland is anyone’s guess, the diplomats concede. But their hope was to give him enough to boast about, even if many of the provisions were implicit in the 1951 agreement and its successors.

Mikkel Runge Olesen, a researcher at the Danish Institute for International Studies, described the final document, which was released on Tuesday, as only a moderate improvement for the United States, achieved at considerable political cost.

“It is an extraordinarily high price to pay for relatively limited changes,” he said, maintaining that Mr. Trump’s threats did lasting damage to relations with Denmark, Greenland and Europe.

The 1951 accord essentially gave the United States the right to build bases across Greenland, and at the height of the Cold War there were more than a dozen. At one point there was even a plan for an under-the-ice nuclear weapons base. But expense, and then the end of the Cold War, led to the abandonment of many of the facilities. Vice President JD Vance visited one of the remaining ones, Pituffik Space Base, in March 2025, declaring that the United States had to “wake up” to China’s and Russia’s designs on the island.

“We can’t just bury our head in the sand,” he said, “or, in Greenland, bury our head in the snow.”

Mr. Vance’s visit touched off even more concern about American intentions. But in recent days, the reactions to the accord have been broadly positive in Denmark and Greenland.

For Naaja Nathanielsen, a member of the Danish Parliament and part of Greenland’s left-leaning pro-independent party, the most significant part of the agreement is the signature page: For the first time, Greenland, alongside Denmark, is a direct signatory of a legally binding international agreement. That was a huge win for Greenland’s population, which has always felt marginalized, constantly debating whether Denmark had its best interests in mind.

“This is the first time we have actually had a seat at the table,” Ms. Nathanielsen said. “That is something we are proud of,” one that she thinks will set a precedent for greater Greenlandic autonomy in foreign policy.

One key change in the new document is an explicit description of how Greenland would be bound by the terms of the accord even if it became independent of Denmark.

“In case Greenland exercises its right to self-determination to become independent, the government of the Kingdom of Denmark and the government of Greenland shall together ensure that the independent Greenlandic state will agree to remain in NATO,” the document says.

item.title: Tropical Sea Turtle Lays Eggs on Southern California Beach
item.description:
With a determined kick of her back flippers, a sea turtle made history on a California beach this month.

For the first time since recordkeeping began, a sea turtle has nested on the West Coast, digging a hole and laying eggs on Sept. 16 near Seal Beach, Calif., about 30 miles south of downtown Los Angeles. The mother was an olive ridley sea turtle, a threatened species most commonly found in tropical and subtropical waters off the coasts of Mexico and India.

Scientists said on Tuesday that the turtle’s arrival was a sign of things to come in California.

The waters off the West Coast have been heating up for years and attracting species accustomed to warmer climes, such as brightly colored tropical sea slugs and Humboldt squid. That trend has been supercharged this year by a major El Niño, a recurring climate pattern characterized by warmer Pacific Ocean temperatures.

Southern California in particular will be a hot spot for unusual sea critter sightings during this El Niño, given the region’s proximity to warmer waters off Mexico and the direction of the currents, said Greg Pauly, curator of herpetology for the Natural History Museum of Los Angeles County.

It could be a remarkable year for spotting marine animals that are rarely seen off the coast of California, such as yellow-bellied sea snakes and sport fish such as wahoo and dorado. Already, local residents this year have observed several hammerhead sharks and two whale sharks, all of which likely were drawn to Southern California by the unusually warm water.

“This is the epicenter,” Dr. Pauly said. “In terms of these things that are pretty spectacular and pretty easy to monitor, this is kind of the place for that.”

Olive ridley sea turtles can live for 50 years and are the smallest type of sea turtle, weighing up to 100 pounds and measuring about three feet in length. Their populations are threatened by commercial fishing nets, habitat loss, changing environmental conditions and other factors.

Sea turtles have been seen in Southern California before and are expanding their range northward as oceans warm, experts say. But none had ever been seen nesting on a beach in Southern California.

Three days after the turtle was seen laying her eggs near Seal Beach last week, a sea turtle was again spotted laying eggs a few miles south, near the Huntington Pier. It is unclear whether it was the same turtle.

Scientists are monitoring the turtle nests through the eggs’ incubation period, which can last for about two months, according to National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration Fisheries. The nests have been fenced and protected, according to the agency.

The expansion of sea turtle nesting sites to new regions is generally viewed as a positive development, since many species are endangered. But there remain many unknowns, such as what will happen when the Southern California waters cool again or how the eggs will be impacted by cooler beach temperatures.

The survival of the hatchlings depends on the temperature of the sand, and even their gender is affected by it. The sex of a turtle isn’t set at fertilization, but determined by the temperature of the egg during incubation, with cooler sand producing more males.

Exciting as it may be, the rare nesting sites come amid a concerning rise in ocean water temperatures because of El Niño, experts say. The temperatures are already breaking records and are still building, with a peak expected later this year.

Peter D. Roopnarine, a California Academy of Sciences paleoecologist who studies how changes in environmental conditions affect ecosystems, said he never expected to be able to study large swings in ocean temperature in real time when he began his research decades ago.

A rise in ocean temperature by a few degrees is considered extreme, and it was once viewed as quick if that took place over thousands of years.

“To actually see this happening within a generation and see El Niños that are sort of kicking up their energy, the only word you can use for it is alarming,” Dr. Roopnarine said.

Scientists say they expect the coming months to bring yellow-bellied sea snakes, a venomous species that is commonly found around the world but typically doesn’t travel as far north as California.

Only six such snakes have ever been collected in the state, five of which came during an El Niño year. And this year, there has already been an unofficial report of one washing ashore in Orange County.

The warming ocean temperature could also be harmful to some species that are native to California. Giant kelp, for example, thrives in cool waters and will likely suffer, as will the southern sea otters that rely on the kelp.

Seals and sea lions could also be harmed because they feed on fish that eat plankton that live in cold, nutrient-rich water and may not be as abundant in warmer temperatures. Already this year, sea lions have washed ashore on California beaches after falling sick from eating fish that had consumed toxic algae that flourishes in warmer water.

“These are really abnormally warm temperatures,” Dr. Pauly said.

item.title: Dispute Over Missouri’s Congressional Map Again Returns to Supreme Court
item.description:
The messy legal battle over Missouri’s congressional map returned late Tuesday to the Supreme Court for a third time this month after a lower court sided with Republicans seeking to use district boundaries redrawn to give the party an advantage in November.

The Supreme Court has twice cleared a path for Missouri to hold its general election under an older map that would likely help Democrats retain both of their congressional seats from the state. Ballots reflecting those voting lines were mailed to overseas and military voters last week.

But a decision Monday night from the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit reopened questions about the map and put the issue back before the justices.

The state’s primary was held in August using the redrawn, pro-Republican map, meaning that as it now stands, many voters would be choosing among general election candidates whom they had no role in nominating.

Proponents of the older map that is more favorable to Democrats asked the Supreme Court on Tuesday night to block the appeals court order that would require the use of the newer, GOP-friendly map. The appeals court had given the justices until next Monday evening to settle which map would be in place for November.

In their filing just before midnight Tuesday, the proponents said ballots using the older map have been printed and mailed, and absentee voting, both by mail and in person, began Tuesday. Without Supreme Court action, they said, “the result is chaos on both sides of Election Day: confusion over how to conduct the election now, and uncertainty over the rules governing its results.”

The justices indicated they would likely move quickly, asking for a response from Republican congressional candidates who sued over the issue by 2 p.m. on Wednesday.

A three-judge panel of the Eighth Circuit on Monday had said that using different maps for the primary and general elections was unconstitutional. The panel ordered the state to use the same map in November that had been used for the primary. They wrote that it would cause “the least amount of confusion for voters subjected to a string of changes this month.”

Missouri was among the states that redrew congressional maps outside the usual once-a-decade cycle at President Trump’s request. The new map, which legislators approved last year during a special session, would position Republicans to flip a Kansas City-area district now held by Democrats, which could help determine control of Congress. Republicans currently hold six of Missouri’s eight U.S. House seats.

The fast-moving fight over the state’s voting lines has led to confusion and uncertainty amid conflicting court rulings. Missouri’s Supreme Court also found that the state’s top election official had been in contempt for not moving quickly enough to implement its order to return to the older map.

Redistricting opponents gathered hundreds of thousands of signatures seeking a statewide referendum on the new map. Secretary of State Denny Hoskins, a Republican, said he believed redistricting was not eligible for a referendum — a decision he announced on Primary Day in August.

The Missouri Supreme Court disagreed, saying the redrawn boundaries were not yet law, and ordered the question to appear on the November ballot for a referendum before the new map was used for a general election. By the time the state Supreme Court ruled, candidates had already campaigned and voters had already cast primary ballots under the redrawn lines.

When the issue reached the U.S. Supreme Court earlier this month, the justices showed little interest in upending a unanimous decision from the state’s highest court on a matter of state law, and in the middle of a heated election season.

The first time, Justice Brett M. Kavanaugh, acting on his own, refused a request from Missouri officials to use the redrawn map. The second time, on Sept. 10, the full court took part in a decision with the same effect. The justices blocked a lower court decision that would have allowed state officials to use the redrawn map. In both instances, the court’s brief orders did not include any reasoning, as is often the case when the justices respond to emergency requests.

But the lack of explanation left an opening for the Eighth Circuit to issue its opinion on the underlying legal questions. Some scholars said on Tuesday that the ruling seemed to circumvent the spirit of the Supreme Court’s earlier orders. At oral arguments last week, the appeals court panel’s presiding judge, James Loken, suggested the justices’ order was a directive for it to act quickly.

“Time is of the essence,” Judge Loken said, adding that the Supreme Court had “told us, ‘Get to work.’”
